issues.legal_issue: A former licensee whose licence has expired may recover possession from the owner through a summary possessory remedy after being dispossessed without consent and otherwise than through lawful process.
material_facts: The bank occupied the premises under an admitted leave-and-licence agreement that expired, and the owner had refused renewal.
The bank stopped conducting business in the premises after a fire and began operating elsewhere; the owner had not used force to remove it.
The bank’s letter described the premises as vacated after the fire, and the owner later restricted access to the premises.
The bank sought recovery of possession through a summary possessory suit.
issues.conclusion: Justice Kasliwal concluded that the bank could not recover possession: in his view, it had vacated because of the fire and had not been dispossessed by force or unlawful means; after the licence expired, it was a trespasser with no right to recover possession from the admitted owner. Justice Ramaswamy reached the opposite conclusion, treating the bank as dispossessed without consent and entitled to recover possession. The judges divided, and the matter was referred to a larger bench; neither view was a majority resolution in this judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act, a person dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law may seek summary recovery of possession without the court determining title. Justice Kasliwal distinguished a tenant holding over, whose possession may receive statutory protection, from a licensee whose licence has expired: relying on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and the quoted passage from K.K. Verma v. Naraindas C. Malkani, and on D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav, he treated the former licensee’s possession as that of a trespasser and denied recovery against the owner on these facts. Justice Ramaswamy disagreed, relying on the purpose of Section 6 to prevent self-help and on authorities including Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, Rudrappa v. Narsingrao, Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, Ram Ratan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. Rev. Father K.C. Alexander, and Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao; he considered settled possession protected even against the owner until lawful eviction.

rule.if: summary_possession_proceeding and former_licensee and licence_expired and owner_title_admitted and occupant_left_after_unavoidable_event and not owner_used_force_to_remove_occupant

predicates.summary_possession_proceeding: The claimant brought a summary suit seeking recovery of possession of immovable property.
predicates.former_licensee: The claimant had entered and occupied the property under a licence granted by the owner.
predicates.licence_expired: The agreed period of the claimant’s licence ended without an agreed renewal.
predicates.owner_title_admitted: The parties admitted that the defendant owned the property.
predicates.occupant_left_after_unavoidable_event: The claimant stopped using the premises and left them after an event made continued business use impracticable.
predicates.owner_used_force_to_remove_occupant: The owner used force to remove the claimant from the property.

issues.definition: In a summary possession proceeding, this view denies recovery where a former licensee’s licence has expired, the owner’s title is admitted, the occupant left after an unavoidable event, and the owner did not use force to remove the occupant.

issues.legal_issue: A person in settled possession who entered lawfully may recover possession through a summary possessory remedy if the owner retakes possession without consent and otherwise than through lawful process, even after the person’s licence has expired.
material_facts: The bank had entered the premises lawfully under a licence and had occupied them for many years.

After the fire, the bank said it surrendered the premises to allow repairs and renovation and that the owner had undertaken to return possession; the bank’s furniture and other items remained in part of the premises.
The bank claimed a continuing intention to possess and sought recovery after the owner refused to restore access.
In the High Court, the owner’s counsel agreed, for purposes of the suit and without prejudice, to proceed on the footing that the bank had been dispossessed as alleged.
The bank brought its summary possessory suit within six months of the alleged dispossession.
issues.conclusion: Justice Ramaswamy concluded that the bank had been dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law, and was entitled to recover possession. Justice Kasliwal disagreed and would have denied relief. Because the judges divided, the matter was referred to a larger bench; Justice Ramaswamy’s conclusion was not a majority resolution in this judgment.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6 of the Specific Relief Act provides a summary remedy for a person dispossessed without consent and otherwise than in due course of law, without regard to either party’s title, if the suit is brought within six months. Section 52 of the Indian Easements Act defines a licence as permission to do something on another’s immovable property without creating an interest in it. Justice Ramaswamy reasoned that, despite the ordinary consequences of an expired licence, settled possession cannot be terminated by self-help and must be ended through lawful process. He relied on Midnapur Zamindary Co. Ltd. v. Naresh Narayan Roy, Rudrappa v. Narsingrao, Munshi Ram v. Delhi Administration, Puran Singh v. State of Punjab, Ram Ratan v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Nair Service Society Ltd. v. Rev. Father K.C. Alexander, Yar Muhammad v. Lakshmi Das, and Krishna Ram Mahale v. Shobha Venkat Rao. He distinguished D.H. Maniar v. Waman Laxman Kudav and rejected the contrary approach attributed to Chandu Lal v. Municipal Corporation of Delhi. Justice Kasliwal took the opposing view, relying on Lallu Yeshwant Singh v. Rao Jagdish Singh and D.H. Maniar.

rule.if: summary_possession_proceeding and lawful_initial_entry and long_peaceful_occupation and claimant_retained_intention_to_possess and owner_repossessed_without_judicial_process and suit_brought_within_six_months

predicates.summary_possession_proceeding: The claimant brought a summary suit seeking recovery of possession of immovable property.
predicates.lawful_initial_entry: The claimant first entered the property with the owner’s permission or under an agreement with the owner.
predicates.long_peaceful_occupation: The claimant occupied the property for an extended period without interruption.
predicates.claimant_retained_intention_to_possess: The claimant continued to assert an intention to possess the property, including by retaining belongings or requesting its return.
predicates.owner_repossessed_without_judicial_proce: The owner took or retained possession without obtaining it through a court or other lawful process.
predicates.suit_brought_within_six_months: The claimant filed the suit within six months after the alleged dispossession.

issues.definition: This view makes summary recovery available when a claimant who entered lawfully and remained in peaceful possession with an ongoing intention to possess is deprived of the property by the owner without judicial process and sues within six months.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory exclusion of appeals and reviews from summary possessory proceedings does not prevent the Supreme Court from exercising its special-leave jurisdiction to examine the resulting decision.
material_facts: The case reached the Supreme Court by special leave from a decree in a summary possessory suit.
The respondent argued that the statutory bar on appeal or review meant that the Supreme Court should not review the High Court’s decree.
issues.conclusion: Justice Ramaswamy rejected the argument, holding that the Supreme Court’s jurisdiction under Article 136 is plenary and is not barred by the statutory prohibition on appeal or review. The judges divided on the principal possession issue and referred the matter to a larger bench.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(3) of the Specific Relief Act bars an appeal or review from an order or decree in a suit under that section. Justice Ramaswamy held that this does not restrict the Supreme Court’s plenary judicial-review jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution.

predicates.special_leave_proceeding: A party sought the Supreme Court’s special-leave jurisdiction to challenge a lower court decision.
predicates.underlying_summary_possession_case: The challenged decision arose from a summary suit for recovery of possession.
predicates.statute_bars_ordinary_appeal_or_review: The governing law prohibits an ordinary appeal or review of the order or decree.

issues.definition: This view means that a statutory bar on ordinary appeals or reviews does not prevent Supreme Court examination through special leave of a decision in a summary possession case.
